title: Articles of Note Week of November 2, 2026
author: Jason Moore
summary: This weekly Articles of Note digest from ON Classical Education, provided by Jason Moore, collects excerpts from roughly eighteen pieces on classical education, schooling and the humanities. The lead item is Christopher Perrin's Closing the Window on Wonder, followed by a Martin Center essay on universities and the Western story and a Wall Street Journal letter on classical education. A large cluster concerns what the midterm results mean for education, drawn from Informed Choice, Chalkbeat, Rick Hess, AEI and National Review. The learning-focused items include Marybeth Gasman on teaching critical reading, a Kelsey Piper and Freddie deBoer debate on whether schools matter, Fordham on the AP dilemma, and Parker Baxter on the first great enrollment decline. It closes with a National Review piece on civics schools and Jonathan Bate on Shakespeare's gardens. Several of these items were also checked individually for archiving.
points: The digest leads with Perrin's reflection on wonder and the loss of it, which fits the classical emphasis on forming the whole person.
Midterm education coverage dominates, with sources disagreeing about whether the results help or hurt school choice and education reform.
Kelsey Piper and Freddie deBoer's exchange tests whether schools can change relative student outcomes, with deBoer arguing that academic rank is largely stable.
Items from Fordham and Education Next examine institutional drift in AP and in district responses to falling enrollment.
The digest closes with civics schools and Jonathan Bate on Shakespeare's gardens, reflecting the humanities and civic formation themes of the classical movement.
quotes: Great nations have always told their children great stories. From Homer and Virgil to the Bible, inherited narratives teach courage, duty, sacrifice, faith, and belonging.
It is remarkable that we can step onto a plane with 200 other people, sit comfortably, and then fly over 1000 miles in a couple of hours at 600 miles per hour.

This contention has been a constant in American educational debates for decades, exemplified by the 2010 documentary Waiting for “Superman” and its triumphalist narrative about charter schools. Unfortunately, this attitude runs into a stark reality: Schools and teachers just don’t have that much impact on relative student outcomes.
Democrats took control of the U.S. Senate and House, and they won governors’ races in Iowa, Texas, Ohio, and Georgia, all previously Republican strongholds.

The policy implications of Tuesday’s historic electoral shift are many and far-reaching, and much ink will be spilled discussing tariffs, the Iran war, and immigration. But one thing is certain: Education reform was significantly set back.
It’s hard to feel sorry for the College Board, so let’s not. But let’s also try to understand an enormous dilemma that this enormous organization faces.
How well do institutional leaders learn from the lessons of the past? If school districts are the institutions in question, the answer is: not well at all.

Across the country, civics schools have emerged as a major force of reform in higher education. These schools, founded by state legislatures and in most cases housed at major public universities, aim to restore serious teaching and scholarship on American civics within an academic establishment that is often hostile to the country’s founding principles and Western heritage.
